disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattention and hyperactive-impulsive behaviors that are inconsistent with developmental level and cause impairment in at least two settings (e.g., work, home, social). Symptoms typically begin in childhood, but in many adults they are only recognized later when occupational, relational, or organizational demands exceed their coping strategies. The course is usually chronic, with fluctuations in severity depending on structure, stress, and environmental supports; some individuals develop compensatory routines that partially mask difficulties until these are overwhelmed. Clinically, it is distinguished from mood, anxiety, and personality disorders by its early onset, pervasiveness across situations, and a core pattern of attentional disorganization and impulse-control difficulties rather than episodic changes in mood or solely situational stress responses.

narrative.stressor: Around two years ago, Maria was promoted to lead several concurrent audit engagements that required long stretches of meticulous review, complex GAAP research, and coordination with a distributed team using new AI-enhanced tools. The higher volume of shifting deadlines and constant email and chat communication gradually overwhelmed the informal systems she had always relied on—late-night catch-up sessions, color-coded spreadsheets, and last-minute sprints—making it harder for her to keep track of key review points and sign-offs. As partners began questioning inconsistencies between her usually spotless workpapers and the final reports, Maria found herself staying later, delaying dance classes and community commitments, and feeling increasingly anxious about missing something critical despite putting in more hours. After nearly losing a major client due to overlooked documentation and receiving her first formal performance warning in over twenty years, she consulted her primary care physician, who referred her for psychiatric evaluation when it became clear that her longstanding focus and follow-through difficulties were now significantly impairing her work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep starting audit tasks and then somehow not finishing them or missing key steps, even when I’m trying my absolute best to follow through.”

narrative.stressor: In the past two years, Dennis’s call center transitioned to stricter performance metrics and a new omnichannel CRM platform that required rapidly switching between phone, chat, and email while following detailed scripts and documentation protocols. The faster pace and constant dashboard alerts made it increasingly difficult for him to keep his place in workflows, remember what he had just agreed to with a customer, and complete tickets accurately, leading to repeated quality flags and tense coaching sessions despite his strong interpersonal skills and product knowledge. The stress began to spill over into his home life; he would intend to tackle simple tasks like organizing bills or finishing DIY projects after work but instead bounced between unfinished chores, leaving his wife to quietly pick up the slack. When he was placed on a performance improvement plan and told that another quarter of documentation errors could jeopardize his job, Dennis, worried about losing their main source of income before retirement, agreed to an employee assistance referral and then pursued a full psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “At work my mind jumps to every little thing going on around me, and I lose track of what I’m doing in the middle of a customer call.”

narrative.stressor: After her husband’s death and subsequent retirement from her role as a senior center coordinator several years ago, Janet gradually filled her days with multiple volunteer projects, church activities, and family commitments. Over the last couple of years, as she took on coordinating the neighborhood garden, organizing oral history interviews, and helping with grandchildren’s schedules, the unstructured nature of her time made it harder for her to keep track of what she had promised to do and when. She found herself double-booking events, misplacing sign-up sheets, and forgetting routine self-care tasks like taking her vitamins or bringing needed materials to quilting meetings, which contrasted sharply with her past reputation for reliability and began to frustrate fellow volunteers and family members. Feeling embarrassed when a church outreach event she had agreed to coordinate nearly fell apart because of overlooked details, she mentioned her growing difficulty managing everyday responsibilities to her primary care doctor, who recommended a psychiatric evaluation to explore underlying attentional issues.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep forgetting everyday things I’m supposed to do, like taking my pills or bringing what I need to church events, even when I write them down.”
